findings.title: The intake API reads request['org_id'] from a middleware that build_app never registers, so no authentication runs on the transfer routes
findings.evidence: build_app constructs `web.Application()` and sets a producer and the routes — there is no middlewares=[...] argument and no app.middlewares.append anywhere in the file or the package. _org_of (line 41) nevertheless returns `request["org_id"]` with the docstring 'Resolved by the auth middleware from the verified workspace token', and the module docstring on line 4 states 'Clients authenticate with a workspace JWT'. No JWT verification code exists anywhere in ledger-stream: grep for jwt, jwks, decode or Authorization finds only the RFC example in the docstring.
findings.impact: POST /v1/transfers and POST /v1/holds are unauthenticated. Since org_id is what stamps the x-org header (line 54) and lands in the payload (line 70), the caller either causes a KeyError 500 or — if any middleware is added later that sets the key permissively — publishes transfers attributed to an org of their choosing. Either way the org attribution the whole downstream policy chain rests on (LS-03) originates from a control that is not in the build.
findings.recommendation: Register the middleware in build_app and make _org_of fail closed — read with request.get('org_id') and raise HTTPUnauthorized when absent, rather than KeyError-ing — so a missing authentication layer produces a 401 rather than an accident. Add a test that posts to /v1/transfers with no Authorization header and asserts 401.

triage.reason: The mandatory layer is exactly what is missing: aiohttp applies only the middlewares passed to web.Application or appended to app.middlewares, and neither happens in this tree. An API gateway in front could authenticate the caller, but it could not populate the aiohttp request mapping this code reads, so no out-of-repo artifact makes _org_of resolve; the finding would move to the gateway's header injection rather than disappear.
build_app is the only application factory in the module and is not behind a flag; there is no separate production factory in the tree.

findings.title: The client-chosen idempotency key becomes the ledger row's primary key on an INSERT OR REPLACE, so a transfer can overwrite an existing entry
findings.evidence: `id=str(payload.get("idempotency_key") or uuid.uuid4())` sets the Entry id from a request field, and store.post_entry executes `INSERT OR REPLACE INTO entries VALUES (...)` (store.py:65) against a table whose id is the PRIMARY KEY (store.py:9). SQLite's OR REPLACE deletes the conflicting row and inserts the new one. The field is unconstrained on the way in: schemas.py:24 declares `idempotency_key: Optional[str] = Field(default=None, max_length=64)` with no pattern, no uniqueness and no binding to the caller.
findings.impact: A caller who learns or guesses an existing entry id — and ids are attacker-chosen for every transfer they have ever submitted, so they know many — submits a transfer with that idempotency_key and silently replaces the stored row, changing its account, org, direction, amount and memo. An idempotency mechanism intended to prevent double-posting becomes a primitive for rewriting posted history, and the daily-limit check at apply.py:55 is defeated too, since replacing rows removes their contribution to the day's sum.
findings.recommendation: Keep the two identities separate: generate the row id server-side and store the idempotency key in its own column with a unique index scoped to the account, then check for an existing key and return the prior result instead of writing. Change the statement to a plain INSERT so a primary-key collision is an error rather than a silent overwrite.

triage.reason: No layer prevents the collision: post_entry's docstring (store.py:63) explicitly delegates policy to the caller, and apply_transfer's checks are on amount, org and daily total — none of them reads whether the id already exists.
idempotency_key is a declared field of TransferRequest (schemas.py:24), populated from the request body at app.py:64 and carried into the payload by model_dump at line 69.
The rows are ledger entries — account, org, direction and amount in cents (store.py:8-16) — which is financial record data, and the overwrite destroys the prior record rather than merely reading it.

findings.title: The settlement backfill writes rows straight to the ledger table, taking entry id and org id from the CSV and applying none of the policy checks the message path enforces
findings.evidence: Two writers reach the entries table. apply_transfer runs signature verification, the topic ceiling, the account-ownership test and the daily limit before post_entry (apply.py:42-56). load/rows_from build tuples directly from csv.DictReader and pass them to store.append_raw (backfill.py:49-50), which executes `INSERT OR REPLACE INTO entries VALUES (?, ...)` for each (store.py:72-74) with no checks at all. Two of the fields come from the file rather than from the operator: `record.get("entry_id") or str(uuid.uuid4())` on line 38 and `record.get("org_id") or org_id` on line 39 — so a column present in the CSV overrides the --org argument the operator supplied.
findings.impact: A settlement export whose rows carry an org_id column writes entries into any org, and one carrying an entry_id column replaces existing ledger rows through OR REPLACE, exactly as LS-06 but in bulk and with no amount ceiling or daily limit. The operator running the tool believes --org scopes the load; the code lets the file override it.
findings.recommendation: Take org_id from the argument only and ignore any column of that name, generate entry ids server-side or namespace them so an import cannot collide with a posted entry, and route the batch through the same policy function the consumer uses — or, at minimum, apply the amount ceiling and the daily limit before append_raw. Use a plain INSERT so a collision surfaces.

triage.reason: The checks exist on the other writer. append_raw's own docstring (store.py:70) names it as the bulk loader for tooling, and it contains no validation; nothing between rows_from and executemany inspects the values.

The values come from the CSV, which is a file produced by an external party — 'a normalised export produced by the settlement bank' per the module docstring (line 3). That is outside the operator's control even though the directory is mounted read-only.
org_id is the tenancy boundary of this system — apply.py:51 rejects a message whose account belongs to a different org — so a file that sets it crosses a boundary between second principals.

findings.title: Unsanitised Kafka header values are interpolated into line-oriented log records
findings.evidence: log_escaper.py flagged this call UNCLEARED with 'arg2:bound `org_id`'. Reading it: org_id is header_value(headers, "x-org") from line 41, and header_value decodes the raw bytes with `value.decode("utf-8", "replace")` (serde.py:34) — a decoder that preserves \r and \n rather than rejecting them. The value reaches `LOG.warning("dropping %s from non-platform org %s", topic, org_id)` with no neutralisation. The tool flagged seven further uncleared sites on the same tree; retry.py:41 and :61 have the same shape with original_topic, which is likewise a header (retry.py:38), and retry.py:58 and consumer.py:90 interpolate a PolicyRejected whose message embeds the caller's account_id (apply.py:52).
findings.impact: A producer sets x-org to a value containing CRLF and writes fabricated records into the worker log — including records that read as a successful application of a message that was actually dropped. Since this is the only trace of a rejected admin-topic message, it is also the audit trail an incident would be reconstructed from. The standard logging formatter emits one line per record, so the forged records are indistinguishable downstream.
findings.recommendation: Neutralise before logging: strip or escape \r and \n from any header-derived value, or switch the logger to a JSON formatter so a newline inside a field cannot become a record boundary. Apply it in header_value, at the single point every header crosses into the application, rather than at each call site.

triage.reason: x-org is a producer-set Kafka header, read verbatim at consumer.py:41 with no allowlist, and the errors='replace' decode at serde.py:34 does not remove control characters.

The sink is line-oriented: LOG is a stdlib logging.Logger (consumer.py:19) with no formatter configured in the tree, so the default one-record-per-line text output applies. A JSON formatter would change this answer, and there is none here.
The deferred %s form is not a defence — WEB-28 records six auditors mistaking exactly that idiom for the safe example. The interpolation happens in the formatter and the newline survives either way.

It is not merely defence in depth: this log line is the only record of a dropped admin-topic message, so forging it defeats detection of the LS-03 attack rather than duplicating a control that exists elsewhere.

findings.title: The consumer commits the offset after an unhandled failure and never produces to the dead-letter topic it declares
findings.evidence: DLQ_TOPIC is declared at consumer.py:21 and `grep -rn DLQ_TOPIC` shows it is never used in that module — no produce call exists anywhere in the tree. The loop catches PolicyRejected (line 89) and bare Exception (line 91), logs, and then falls through to `consumer.commit(msg, asynchronous=False)` on line 93, which is outside the try and therefore runs on every path including the failure ones. enable.auto.commit is False (line 32), so this is the only commit.
findings.impact: A message that fails to apply — for a transient store error as much as for a policy rejection — is committed and never reprocessed, and does not reach the DLQ that retry.py subscribes to (retry.py:68). The replay worker therefore consumes a topic nothing produces to, which is both a silent-loss path for genuine failures and the reason the LS-05 assumption ('already checked by the main consumer before being parked') describes a flow that does not exist. Bounding (recorded rather than invoked as an exculpation, since an exculpation that holds would rule the finding out): This is an availability and audit-integrity defect rather than a path an attacker directly exploits, so it is bounded to low; per FP-10 it is still written down, because it is what makes the retry worker's trust assumption (LS-05) false.
findings.recommendation: Produce the failed message, with its headers and an x-original-topic and x-attempts, to DLQ_TOPIC before committing, and commit only after the message is either applied or successfully parked. Distinguish PolicyRejected (a permanent rejection, do not replay) from an unexpected exception (transient, replay) rather than treating both the same.

triage.reason: run() is the module's deployed entry point, not a test path, and the commit is unconditional in the shipped loop.

A broker-side or connector-side dead-letter mechanism could park failures without application code. Nothing in the tree configures one — build_consumer sets four keys and none of them is dead-letter related (consumer.py:29-34) — so per FP-08 this stays UNKNOWN, which is why the finding is low rather than higher.

findings.title: Command injection: the diagnostic endpoint interpolates a query parameter into a shell command line
findings.evidence: `exec.CommandContext(ctx, "sh", "-c", "ping -c 1 -W 2 "+host)` where host is `r.URL.Query().Get("host")` from line 15. The only check is the non-empty test on line 16. Because the command is handed to `sh -c` as a single string, every shell metacharacter is live: `?host=x;id`, `?host=$(...)`, `?host=x|nc ...`. CombinedOutput is then returned to the caller in the JSON response (line 28), so the command's stdout and stderr come back in the body. The sibling handler one function down, handleResolve, shows the safe shape: net.DefaultResolver.LookupHost with no shell at all.
findings.impact: Arbitrary command execution as the objects service inside the mesh, with the output returned to the attacker — a full interactive foothold, not a blind one. The route needs no credential (MG-05) and, per MG-02, is reachable from the host because the container publishes its port; the Envoy RBAC that was meant to confine /internal/ is on a different path (MG-04 covers the /admin variant of the same mistake).
findings.recommendation: Drop the shell: `exec.CommandContext(ctx, "ping", "-c", "1", "-W", "2", host)` passes host as a single argv element that no shell parses. Beyond that, validate host as an IP or DNS name before use, and put the whole diagnostic surface behind an authorization check.

triage.reason: Nothing sits between the query read and the exec: the two statements are lines 15 and 24 of the same function, with only the empty test and a context timeout between them. The Envoy RBAC rule is an external layer and MG-02 establishes it can be bypassed; per FP-01 a control a caller can route around is not this rule.
host is a URL query parameter, read directly with r.URL.Query().Get and used with no allowlist, regex or type conversion.

The benign reading would be that exec.Command's argv model prevents shell parsing. It does — but only when the binary is the command; here the binary is `sh` and `-c` makes the concatenated string a script, which is the documented exception.

findings.title: The object service publishes its port to the host, so every request can bypass Envoy's RBAC and ext_authz and self-assert its identity headers
findings.evidence: The objects service declares `ports: - "8081:8081"` alongside its mesh network address, publishing the backend on the host in addition to the edge proxy's 8080. The Go service's entire identity model is header-based: principalFrom (auth.go:22-37) reads X-Fleet-User, X-Fleet-Tenant and X-Fleet-Roles from the request, and requireRole (line 52) derives every authorization decision from them. The single place those headers are prevented from being self-asserted is envoy.yaml:63-66, `request_headers_to_remove` on the public virtual host — a control that only applies to traffic that goes through Envoy.
findings.impact: A request to host:8081 with `X-Fleet-User: x`, `X-Fleet-Tenant: <victim tenant>` and `X-Fleet-Roles: admin` is fully authorized: it reads and writes any tenant's objects (main.go:58, 76), reaches the operator surface at /admin (MG-05) and the command injection at /internal/diag (MG-01). Every control in the envoy configuration — the RBAC subnet rule, the ext_authz session check, the header stripping — is bypassed by not using the proxy.
findings.recommendation: Remove the ports mapping so the objects service is reachable only on the mesh network, as sessiond already is (it declares no ports). Then stop treating a header as proof of identity even inside the mesh: have the service verify the session token itself, or authenticate the proxy to the service with mTLS so a header is trusted only on a connection that proved it came from Envoy.

triage.reason: The header strip is the control and it lives in the proxy, which this path does not traverse. The Go service performs no equivalent: auth.go has no code path that rejects a self-asserted header, and main.go registers the mux directly on the listener with only withCache in front.

The intended exposure is the edge listener on 8080 (docker-compose.yml:10), which is the one the architecture describes. 8081 is the backend's own port and nothing in the tree presents it as a public surface — the comment at envoy.yaml:62 states the opposite: 'Identity is stamped by sessiond, never by the client.'
Tenants are second principals throughout: store.go:56 refuses a write whose tenant differs, main.go:67 refuses a read whose meta.Tenant differs, and List filters by tenant (store.go:115).

findings.title: The partner virtual host disables ext_authz and does not strip the identity headers the public host removes
findings.evidence: public_vh carries `request_headers_to_remove: [x-fleet-user, x-fleet-roles, x-fleet-tenant]` (lines 63-66) and runs ext_authz. partner_vh (lines 73-86) has neither: it sets typed_per_filter_config disabling ext_authz outright (lines 78-81), and declares no request_headers_to_remove, while routing /v1/ to the same object_service cluster as the public host (lines 83-86). Nothing in the configuration translates the partner's client certificate into the x-fleet-* headers the upstream trusts — there is no lua filter, no header_to_metadata filter and no set_current_client_cert_details.
findings.impact: A request to partners.example.com/v1/objects/<key> carrying `X-Fleet-Tenant: <any tenant>` and `X-Fleet-Roles: admin` reaches the object service with those headers intact and is authorized as that tenant's admin, because auth.go:22 reads them at face value. The comment at lines 75-77 explains why the session check is skipped — partners are identified by mTLS at the load balancer — but that identity is never converted into anything the backend consults, so the route is both unauthenticated at the proxy and self-asserting at the backend.
findings.recommendation: Add the same request_headers_to_remove list to partner_vh so no caller can supply the identity headers, and derive the partner's identity in the proxy from the validated certificate — set_current_client_cert_details plus a filter that maps the subject to x-fleet-tenant — so the backend receives an identity Envoy stamped, matching what the public host does.

triage.reason: The header strip is per-virtual-host and this host does not declare it; Envoy applies request_headers_to_remove only where configured. The upstream applies nothing: auth.go has no rejection path for a self-asserted header.

The intended exposure is a partner reaching /v1/ under their own certificate identity. Reaching it as an arbitrary tenant admin is not bounded by anything: the route has no tenant restriction and points at the same cluster as public traffic.

The load balancer that terminates partner mTLS is outside this repository and could conceivably strip the headers itself. No such configuration arrived, so per FP-08 that is UNKNOWN, never HOLDS. The finding stands on the configuration fact — one virtual host strips and its sibling does not — which is decidable inside envoy.yaml.

findings.title: The Envoy RBAC rule denies the prefix '/admin/' while the operator handler is registered at the exact path '/admin'
findings.evidence: The RBAC policy denies requests to `url_path: { path: { prefix: "/admin/" } }` from principals outside 10.20.0.0/16 (lines 28-33). The Go mux registers `mux.HandleFunc("/admin", srv.handleAdmin)` (main.go:118) — a pattern without a trailing slash, which Go's ServeMux matches exactly and not as a subtree. A request for `/admin` therefore does not carry the prefix `/admin/`, is not matched by the policy, and is not denied; it routes through public_vh's catch-all `prefix: "/"` (envoy.yaml:68) to object_service and reaches handleAdmin. The sibling rule on line 27 does not have this problem: every internal handler is registered under `/internal/...` (main.go:119-121), which the prefix covers.
findings.impact: The whole operator surface is reachable from the internet through the edge listener, without the mesh-subnet restriction the rule exists to impose. handleAdmin then performs no authorization of its own (MG-05), so a GET returns the metadata of every object of every tenant and a POST restores arbitrary objects (MG-06) or dumps any named tenant's listing.
findings.recommendation: Match the route as it is registered: add an exact `path: "/admin"` permission beside the prefix one, or register the handler as `/admin/` in the mux so path and policy agree. More durably, derive both from one source and add a test that replays each registered route against the RBAC policy — the mismatch is invisible in either file alone.

triage.reason: The ext_authz filter after it does not compensate: it establishes a session identity for public_vh but has no path-based rule, and MG-05 shows handleAdmin never consults the resulting headers at all.
Both artifacts ship: envoy.yaml is bind-mounted read-only into the edge container (docker-compose.yml:8) and main.go:118 is in the built service image.

The reading that would save it is that Go redirects /admin to /admin/. It redirects the other way: a registered '/admin' pattern makes ServeMux 301 '/admin/' to '/admin', not the reverse, so the covered form bounces to the uncovered one.

findings.title: The operator and diagnostic handlers perform no authorization at all, while the object handler beside them calls requireRole on both methods
findings.evidence: requireRole is defined at auth.go:52 and has exactly two call sites, main.go:58 and main.go:76, both inside handleObject. handleAdmin (admin.go:22), adminOverview (line 47), restoreSnapshot (line 58), handleStats (main.go:98), handleDiag (diag.go:14) and handleResolve (diag.go:34) call neither requireRole nor principalFrom — none of them reads the caller's identity in any form. The asymmetry is inside one service and one mux registration block (main.go:117-121). The stated control is again a comment: admin.go:19-21 calls it 'the whole operator surface' and diag.go:12 says operators use it, with no code enforcing who an operator is.
findings.impact: Anything that reaches the port drives the operator surface: adminOverview returns Store.Snapshot(), the metadata map for every tenant (store.go:122-125); action "usage" lists any tenant named in the body (admin.go:41); action "restore" writes arbitrary objects (MG-06); "purge-cache" clears the cache. Combined with MG-04 the surface is reachable from the internet and with MG-02 directly on the host port.
findings.recommendation: Call requireRole at the top of every handler that is not deliberately public, with a role the operator console holds, rather than relying on where the request came from. Register the mux behind a wrapper that fails closed for any path not explicitly listed as public, so a newly added handler is protected by default.

triage.reason: No layer covers them in-process: the only middleware is withCache (main.go:125), which does no authentication and in fact serves cached responses without invoking the handler at all (MG-07). Envoy is the external layer and MG-02 and MG-04 show two ways around it.

The claimed bound is mesh-internal reachability. Even granting it, FP-05 says the finding moves rather than disappears — any workload inside the mesh, including a compromised sidecar, gets the full operator surface with no credential.
Second principals are explicit: Snapshot returns objects across tenants and "usage" takes the tenant from the request body, so one caller reads another tenant's records.

findings.title: restoreSnapshot writes through putRaw, which skips the tenant-ownership and quota checks that Put enforces, and takes the object metadata from the request body
findings.evidence: Put (store.go:52-74) refuses a write whose key already belongs to another tenant (`if existing, ok := s.meta[meta.Key]; ok && existing.Tenant != meta.Tenant { return errNotOwner }`) and refuses one that would exceed quotaBytes, then computes Size and Checksum server-side. putRaw (lines 78-88) does none of these: it calls writeBlob and assigns `s.meta[meta.Key] = meta` directly. Its caller is restoreSnapshot (admin.go:58-66), which iterates `req.Objects` — decoded straight from the request body, where adminEntry embeds the full ObjectMeta struct including Tenant, Owner, Size and Checksum (admin.go:14-17). The only bound on the request is a 32 MiB body limit (admin.go:29).
findings.impact: A caller of the admin surface — which is unauthenticated (MG-05) and internet-reachable (MG-04) — overwrites any tenant's object by naming its key with their own tenant string, or reassigns ownership of an existing key by supplying different metadata, since the meta map entry is replaced wholesale. Quota is bypassed and the stored Checksum is whatever the caller claims rather than what was written, so the X-Object-Checksum returned on read (main.go:72) can be made to disagree with the bytes.
findings.recommendation: Have the restore path go through Put so one validator governs both writers, or replicate its checks in putRaw. Recompute Size and Checksum from the body rather than accepting them, and require the restored metadata's tenant to match the authenticated caller's tenant rather than reading it from the payload.

triage.reason: The ownership and quota checks are the controls and they are on the sibling writer: `grep -n putRaw` shows one call site, admin.go:61, and it does not call Put. Neither restoreSnapshot nor handleAdmin performs an equivalent check.
meta is `entry.Meta` from the decoded adminRequest (admin.go:28-32), i.e. the JSON request body, with every field caller-chosen.

The benign reading is the comment at store.go:76-77: 'the metadata comes from a previous export of this same store'. That is an assumption about the caller, not a property of the input — nothing signs the export or marks it as this store's, and adminOverview hands out the snapshot to anyone who asks.

findings.title: The response cache is keyed by path alone and serves hits before the handler runs, so one tenant's object is returned to another and to callers with no identity at all
findings.class: Cross-tenant data exposure via cache key
findings.evidence: `key := r.URL.Path` — the identity headers the response varies on are not in the key, and no Vary handling exists. On a hit the middleware writes the stored status, headers and body and returns (lines 82-92) without calling next.ServeHTTP, so handleObject's requireRole (main.go:58) and its `meta.Tenant != p.Tenant` check (line 67) never execute. The middleware wraps the whole mux (main.go:125), so it also caches /admin GET responses — adminOverview's cross-tenant snapshot — and /internal/stats. Entries are stored whenever the recorded status is 200 (cache.go:97), which is exactly the authorized-success case.
findings.impact: Tenant A reads their object at /v1/objects/k; for the next 20 seconds (main.go:36) any caller requesting that path receives A's object bytes and its X-Object-Checksum header — including a caller with no X-Fleet-* headers at all, since the unauthenticated request is answered from cache before requireRole can reject it. The same mechanism serves the operator snapshot from /admin to anyone who asks within the window.
findings.recommendation: Include every input the response varies on in the key — at minimum the tenant, and the roles if they affect the body — and do not cache responses to authenticated requests without also re-running the authorization check on a hit. Safest here: move the cache inside handleObject, after requireRole and the tenant comparison, so a hit is only ever served to a caller already proven entitled to it, and skip caching entirely for /admin and /internal.

triage.reason: The tenant check is inside the handler and the hit path skips the handler by construction — cache.go:92 returns before next.ServeHTTP on line 95 is reached. There is no authorization anywhere in the middleware.
Tenants are second principals: store.go:15 defines errNotOwner and main.go:67 returns 404 when meta.Tenant differs, so the code itself draws the boundary the cache erases.
The cached bodies are tenant object contents and, for /admin, the metadata of every object in the store — not public content.

findings.title: Cached entries are never evicted on expiry, so the response cache grows without bound
findings.evidence: get treats an expired item as a miss (`if !ok || time.Now().After(item.expiresAt)`) but does not delete it, and no sweeper exists — the only deletions are in purge (line 47), which is called with the fixed prefix "/v1/objects/" from admin.go:38 and :67 and with a per-key prefix from main.go:90. Nothing removes an entry for any other path, and nothing bounds len(c.items). Bodies are stored whole (cache.go:101) and the object PUT limit is 64 MiB (main.go:80).
findings.impact: A caller issuing GETs against many distinct paths accumulates entries indefinitely; every 200 response is retained in full, so the process memory grows until the container is killed. Reachable without a credential where MG-07 applies, since a cached 200 is served and re-stored per key. Bounding (recorded rather than invoked as an exculpation, since an exculpation that holds would rule the finding out): It is an availability defect with no confidentiality or integrity consequence of its own, and the TTL check does prevent stale data being served, so the impact is bounded to resource growth. Severity set to low on that basis; the finding is still recorded.
findings.recommendation: Delete the entry on the expired branch in get, and bound the map — an LRU with a maximum entry count and a maximum total byte size — so a caller cannot choose how much memory the process holds. Consider not caching bodies above a size threshold at all.

triage.reason: No layer bounds it: the cache has no size field (cache.go:20-24) and neither the http.Server settings (main.go:123-128) nor the compose file sets a memory limit.
The affected principal is every other tenant served by the process, since exhausting it takes the shared service down.

findings.title: Object keys share one namespace across tenants, so a write conflict reveals that another tenant holds a given key
findings.evidence: Both s.meta and the ownership test are keyed by meta.Key alone, not by tenant+key: `s.meta[meta.Key]` on lines 56 and 72, and Get looks up `s.meta[key]` ignoring its own tenant argument (line 100). Put returns errNotOwner when the existing entry belongs to another tenant, and handleObject surfaces that as `http.Error(w, err.Error(), http.StatusConflict)` (main.go:87) — err.Error() being the literal string 'object belongs to another tenant'.
findings.impact: A tenant PUTs candidate keys and distinguishes 409 with that message from 201, enumerating which keys other tenants hold and receiving explicit confirmation that the collision is cross-tenant. Object keys often encode customer or document identifiers, so the namespace itself is information. The read side is correctly defended — main.go:67 returns 404 rather than leaking — which is what makes the write side's disclosure stand out. Bounding (recorded rather than invoked as an exculpation, since an exculpation that holds would rule the finding out): The disclosure is one bit per probed key and no content is exposed, so it is bounded well below the confidentiality impact of MG-07. Severity set to low; the finding is still written down because the fix — namespacing the map — also removes a cross-tenant write dependency.
findings.recommendation: Key the maps by tenant and key together, so tenants have independent namespaces and no collision is possible; then a conflict can only be with the caller's own object. Return a generic 409 without the internal error string in any case — err.Error() should not reach the response body.

triage.reason: The ownership check is what produces the oracle rather than preventing it: it correctly blocks the write and then reports precisely why.
What leaks is the existence of another tenant's object under a specific key, plus the fact that the two tenants are distinct — metadata about a second principal's holdings, not public data.

findings.title: An unauthenticated endpoint performs DNS resolution of a caller-supplied name
findings.evidence: `addrs, err := net.DefaultResolver.LookupHost(ctx, name)` with name from `r.URL.Query().Get("name")` (line 35) and no allowlist. The handler returns only whether resolution succeeded and how many addresses came back (lines 45-49), and the comment on lines 32-33 correctly notes that nothing is dialled — which is why this is low rather than a full SSRF. Like its neighbours it calls no authorization function (MG-05).
findings.impact: An outbound DNS query to a name the caller chooses, issued from inside the mesh by an unauthenticated caller: an out-of-band channel usable to confirm reachability, to exfiltrate small amounts of data in the queried label from a foothold elsewhere, and to map the resolver's view of internal names by comparing resolved/unresolved. Bounding (recorded rather than invoked as an exculpation, since an exculpation that holds would rule the finding out): The response discloses only a boolean and a count, and no connection is made to the resolved address, so the impact stops at an out-of-band signalling channel rather than reaching internal services. Severity set to low; per FP-10 the finding is still recorded, and it should be re-rated if the handler ever starts dialling.
findings.recommendation: Authorize the handler as MG-05 recommends, and constrain the name to the internal domains an operator would legitimately debug rather than accepting any string. Returning the count is already the right instinct — keep it, and do not add address disclosure.

triage.reason: No allowlist or authorization precedes the call: the two statements between the query read and LookupHost are the empty check and the context timeout.
name is a URL query parameter used verbatim.
